new_statements.quote: Synchronically, Merap and Murik could not be more different. Merap has strong word-final stress, 26 vowels including diphthongs, triphthongs, length, and nasality distinctions, while Murik is a conservative language, even by Kayanic standards, and has weak penultimate stress with a standard six vowel inventory of i, e, a, o, u, and ə.
new_statements.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. The Languages of Borneo: A Comprehensive Classification. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa, section 2.2.2 'Murik-Merap'.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (pdfinfo: 724 pp., Word 2010, created 2017-04-05; title page 'The Languages of Borneo: A Comprehensive Classification... May 2017, By Alexander D. Smith, Dissertation Committee: Robert Blust, Chairperson'). extracted text of PDF pages 92-93 = printed pp. 62-63, section '2.2.2 Murik-Merap'. The quoted passage is there verbatim, running across the p. 62/63 page break: 'Synchronically, Merap and Murik could not be more different. Merap has strong word-final stress, 26 vowels including diphthongs, triphthongs, | length, and nasality distinctions, while Murik is a conservative language, even by Kayanic standards, and has weak penultimate stress with a standard six vowel inventory of i, e,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Murik proper (Ngorek of Long Semiang, Baram, Sarawak) has weak, non-contrastive stress on the penultimate syllable; the Merap dialect (Langap, Malinau, N. Kalimantan) has shifted to strong, invariant final stress (Smith 2017 OL 56:158: 'In Merap, stress appears regularly on the final syllable').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Murik/Ngorek. For Merap: 'words with CVCCVC structures receive a secondary stress in Merap: ˌCVCˈCVC' (Smith 2017 OL 56:159; dissertation p. 72).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Murik. For Merap: no stressed schwa; historical final-syllable schwa took stress and lowered to a (halaŋ [haˈlaŋ]); vowel clusters like kiawə̯ stressed [kiˈawə̯].
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation-form elicitation (Smith's own fieldwork at Long Semiang, 2014-2018). The Murik statement is a one-sentence characterisation in a subgrouping chapter, not a full phonology section; Blust 2013 notes generally that Borneo stress is non-phonemic and that some interior Sarawak languages show final stress only in citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog muri1259 'Murik (Malaysia)' [mxr] covers Murik proper = Ngorek of Long Semiang (Baram, Sarawak; Smith's consultants prefer 'Ngorek', fn. 4 p. 62 and OL fn. 11 p. 162) and, as a dialect, Merap (mera1243; Langap, Malinau, N. Kalimantan). The two differ sharply in stress: Murik/Ngorek weak penultimate (the quoted statement), Merap strong invariant final stress with secondary stress on CVC initial syllables (Smith 2017 OL 56(1):158-159; dissertation pp. 68, 72). Kalimantan Murik varieties Pua' and Huang Bau (Soriente 2003) are not described for stress in any opened source. The earlier scan verdict NO-SOURCE-FOUND is superseded.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.2 Murik-Merap, pp. 62-63: 'Merap has strong word-final stress... while Murik is a conservative language, even by Kayanic standards, and has weak penultimate stress with a standard six vowel inventory of i, e, a, o, u, and ə.' sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. Merap historical phonology in the context of a central Bornean linguistic area. Oceanic Linguistics 56(1):143-180. doi:10.1353/ol.2017.0006
sources.note: Merap (dialect of muri1259) only: p. 158 'In Merap, stress appears regularly on the final syllable'; p. 159 'words with CVCCVC structures receive a secondary stress in Merap: ˌCVCˈCVC'; p. 174-175 Merap and Sa'ban 'shifted stress to the final syllable' while Ngorek (Murik proper) 'remained relatively unchanged'. Fn. 11 p. 162: Blust 1974 'Murik' of Long Semiyang = Ngorek. No explicit Ngorek stress rule in the article.
